newsitem.title: SWEDEN: European royalty join Sweden to mourn Prince Bertil.
newsitem.headline: European royalty join Sweden to mourn Prince Bertil.

text.p: Church bells rang out across Stockholm on Monday as Sweden paid its last respects to Prince Bertil, the grand old man of Sweden's royal family.
Over 600 guests, including representatives from all European royal families, travelled to Stockholm to attend the first royal funeral in Sweden since the death of King Gustaf VI Adolf in 1973.
The guests included Britain's Prince Philip, Denmark's Queen Margrethe, Norway's King Harald, Spain's Princess Christina, and Princess Margriet from the Netherlands.

The popular Prince Bertil, who was the reigning King Carl XVI Gustaf's uncle and fourth in line to the throne, died in his sleep at his Stockholm home eight days ago, aged 84, after ailing for several years.
His wife, Princess Lilian, a divorced British actress, was by his side when he died.
The love story between Prince Bertil, the third-born son of King Gustav VI Adolf, and Welsh-born Lilian Craig touched hearts across the world.
After meeting and falling in love in London during World War Two, the pair kept their relationship secret for 33 years for the sake of the Swedish crown and to forestall a constitutional crisis.
Prince Bertil's elder brother and heir to the throne, Prince Gustaf Adolf, had died in a plane crash in 1947 while the next brother, Sigvard, waived his right to the throne by marrying a commoner.
Prince Bertil became next in line until his nephew, Crown Prince Carl Gustaf, the infant son of Prince Gustaf Adolf, came of age.

If Prince Bertil had married a commoner he would have had to renounce his right to the throne. This could have meant the throne falling vacant, raising the prospect of a republic if the king died before the crown prince came of age.
The crown prince became king in 1973 and Prince Bertil and Lilian finally married in 1976.
The day of his funeral began with churches all over Stockholm ringing their bells for 30 minutes as day broke to signal the start of the official day of mourning.
Flags all over the city were at half mast as guests gathered at the palace in central Stockholm, bringing traffic in the city centre to a standstill.
The funeral service was to be held in the palace's chapel, conducted by Sweden's Archbishop Gunnar Weman.
A funeral procession, televised live, was then to make its way to the royal graveyard at Haga, outside Stockholm, accompanied by over 900 soldiers and officials and 400 police.
